title: Cap. III Rat. 3: king’s prize — no glory-decree before victory / perseverance foresight
pass_a_gloss: Reason 3. In the divine will the order of acts is considered not in itself, but from a certain analogy to the human will: whence according to our mode of understanding we affirm something earlier, something later as willed or foreseen by God. This having been posited, Vasquez contends: Just as when some king proposes a prize to those contending well, by that law that no one obtain it unless he be victor, he never decrees to anyone, however beloved, to give that prize before he sees him possessed of the victory; so it must be thought of God, that he never decrees to anyone the prize of eternal glory, which he promised as a crown to those contending lawfully, except after the intuition of victory, that is, of perseverance in good works. But now because God is foreknower of all futures, from eternity he foresaw who would carry off the victory, and therefore from eternity from this foresight he decreed to give them glory: just as a prince, when he sees someone has conquered, then at last decides to assign him the prize.
pass_b_english: Rat. 3. In God’s will the order of acts is not read in itself but by analogy to human willing — so in our way of speaking we call one thing prior and another later as willed or foreseen by God. On that footing Vasquez presses: as a king who sets a prize for those who contend well, on the rule that only the victor takes it, never decrees to give that prize to anyone — however loved — before he sees him possessed of the victory, so of God: he never decrees to anyone the prize of eternal glory (promised as a crown to those who contend lawfully) except after intuition of victory, that is perseverance in good works. And since God foreknows all futures, from eternity he foresaw who would win, and from that foresight decreed to give them glory — as a prince, seeing someone has conquered, only then resolves to assign the prize.
source_text: Rat. 3. In Divina voluntate ordo actuum consideratur non per se, sed ex analogia quadam ad voluntatem humanam: unde secundum nostrum intelligendi modum aliquid prius, aliquid posterius a Deo volitum sive praevisum affirmamus. Hoc posito contendit Vasques, Sicuti cum Rex aliquis proponit premium bene certantibus, ea lege ut nullus illo potiatur nisi qui victor sit, nunquam decernit alicui, quantumvis amato, dare illud premium, antequam illum videat victoria potitum; ita de Deo sentiendum, nunquam illum decernere alicui premium aeternae gloriae, quod tanquam coronam promisit legitime certantibus, nisi post intuitum victoriae, hoc est, perseverantiae in bonis operibus. Jam vero quia Deus est praescius omnium futurorum, ab aeterno praevidit quinam victoriam reportabunt, atque idcirco ab aeterno ex hac praevisione decrevit illis dare gloriam: sicuti princeps, cum videt aliquem vicisse, tum demum statuit illi premium assignare.
